-- taste without milk: 7/10 (kinda peanut buttery crunchy rounds)

-----------
haven't tried this for my dog yet, but was going to purchase until i saw the recent news articles in google.
-----------

diamond pet foods is expanding a voluntary recall to include puppy food over possible salmonella contamination, according to the u.s. food and drug administration.

the latest recall, announced monday, covers diamond puppy formula dry dog food manufactured by diamond pet foods in gaston, s.c. the puppy food was distributed in the following 12 states: alabama, florida, georgia, kentucky, maryland, michigan, north carolina, ohio, pennsylvania, south carolina, tennessee and virginia.

this is the third voluntary recall for the company this month. on april 6, the company recalled diamond naturals lamb & rice dry dog food made over possible salmonella contamination. on april 26, the company expanded the recall to its chicken soup for the pet lover's soul adult light formula dry dog food.
so far, no dog illnesses have been reported, the fda said.

pets infected with salmonella can become lethargic and have diarrhea or bloody diarrhea, fever and vomiting, according to the fda. infected pets can also pass the illness on to other animals or humans. pet owners also can contract the illness from handling contaminated pet products, especially if they have not thoroughly washed their hands after handling the pet food.

i've tried many different starbucks coffees, from morning blends to more flavored coffees and not one have i enjoyed or liked.

the vanilla flavor in starbucks natural fusions is a joke. when you first open the bag you are hit with this amazing aroma of nice fragrant coffee with a delightful hint of vanilla. when brewing, you completely loose the vanilla smell. and once tasted, the vanilla is gone. and i don't think i should be expected to have to add something (be it milk, cream, or some other product) to bring out the flavor of the coffee. a good coffee can stand alone straight from the pot.

no matter how weak or strong i made it, it had a not so pleasant taste to it. i'm thinking that it had a lot of quakers in it before the coffee was ground, thus this odd taste was present.

the only redeeming quality is the look and design of the bag, initial smell, and the fact that it gives me my caffeine for the day, even if i have to chug it.

back to the drawing board starbucks and come back with a better tasting blend.

pros:
smells great!
didn't get a bitter taste from it (oddly enough).

cons:
didn't taste like vanilla by any stretch.
isn't all that palatable to my or three other peoples taste.
pricey for mediocre coffee.

review: ... in fact it might just be the exact same formula as your closest local/national grocery store brand but with the added bonus of costing about 30% more. we had recently been using this formula until we ran out and i had to make an emergency run to the local grocery store for a quick replacement. the closest thing they had was their organic store brand. funny thing is, when i got home to compare the two i noticed the ingredients are exactly the same as well as some of the machine writing on the bottom of the cans where you can find the sell by date. from what i can gather after doing a bit of research the formula ingredients used to be different but have recently changed without letting customers know. virtually all store brand organic formulas come from one manufacturing plant whether you buy it at store x or y and it seems that earth's best is now being produced in this same facility but charging a premium price. i suggest checking this out for yourself, you might be able to save some money.

review:
... in his famous dictionary of 1755, when he defined "oats" as a grain eaten in england by horses and in scotland by people. well, i guess i'm not scottish. i've never regarded hot oatmeal as more than a cruel necessity of back-packing, and i've hated cold bran flakes -- honestly, all cold cereals -- since i was a child accustomed to swedish cheese-and-herring breakfasts. but i'm adaptable. when i lived in japan, i learned to 'relish' cold rice, raw egg, and dried seaweed for breakfast. it was easier in spain, where hot chocolate and churros for dunking, in my neighborhood cafetería, seemed quite an elegant solution to the problem of mornings. best of all was italy: a huge bowl of caffe latte and a couple of croissants! but wait! mexico was breakfast heaven: huevos rancheros, fried eggs on black beans and tortillas with melted cheese and hot sauce!

yes, i've had to confront the curse of mornings in a lot of environments, but now i'm living in the strangest realm of all: mortality, to which i hold the civic rights of senior citizenship. and i'm striving to be responsible, eating closer to my small share of the world's nutritional resources. oat bran is reputed to reduce cholesterol - mine is unexpectedly high now - and to support a healthy colon. well, a healthy colon is nothing to scoff at, in every way superior to a colon burdened with diverticula as labyrinthine as the intellectual diverticula of life in the usa.

these arrowhead mills oat bran flakes are 100% unsugared, unflavored, unadulterated horse food. i like that in a cereal to be eaten for duty rather than pleasure. mixed with blueberries or raspberries, they're acceptably neutral, like the gesso on a painter's canvas before the pigments are applied. but you have to eat them quickly! don't even try to read the sports page until you've gobbled them down! if they get soggy in the milk, they become as repulsive as canned spinach or truck-stop mashed potatoes.

are they effective for reducing cholesterol? i can't say. i bought my 'pack of 4' and consumed my daily portion until the last box was empty, but that was probably not a long enough test trial to certify or decertify the product. on the other hand, i can testify to their utility for weight loss; i had no temptation to gobble a second bowlful.

review:
... jarred and vacuum-packed chestnuts may be close enough to the real thing to deceive your palate. the real thing is increasingly problematical in the usa, available only part of the year at best, often of poor quality, sometimes of such terrible quality that you'll give up on chestnuts forever. and of course, even if you can get good chestnuts, they are hard work to prepare in sufficient quantity for many recipes. this offering, by the way, is shockingly expensive; the same or similar imported jarred chestnuts are sold in my local markets in sf for half this price or less.

one of my cage-mates in the amazoo requested this recipe:
equal quantities of roasted chestnuts and fresh brussels sprouts.
roast and peel the chestnuts (or use these pale substitutes from the jar).
steam the sprouts, but somewhat less than completely.
braise the chestnuts and sprouts together in an ample amount of unsalted butter, with just a hint of garlic (not powder of course!), until the sprouts take a bit of brown color.
serve hot.
very well matched with a puree of potatoes and celery root, and roasted duck.

well, a lot has changed since then. the filling texture seems margarine-y to me (somewhat like whipped crisco) rather than the creamy, melt-in-your-mouth goodness i remember. also, the flavor seems less pronounced, and the hazelnuts are definitely not as fresh and crunchy as they once were.

maybe it's just me, or perhaps this is a shipping version of the recipe, better suited to handle temperature swings and rough handling. whatever the reason, i wouldn't pay $66 for 1.5 lb box again; $25-30 seems about right.

review:

i wish i'd looked at the ingredient label before ordering this on vine, this is not suitable for my dog, or anyone's in my opinion.

benefil does have beautiful packaging and an excellent top closure. but i don't want to pick up up the giant "fluffy floaters" produced by a corn-heavy dog diet, nor do i want my dog to suffer digestive system pressure while processing this food. i gave my dog 1/2 cup of benefil and then threw in the towel given the immediate fluffy-floaters produced.

purina should go back to the drawing board on this one.

review:
... well, actually you can but the results will be something less than stellar. well, imagine someone did that and then complained about the quality of the nails they received. that is what is happening with some (but not all) of the bad reviews here.

coffee pods are made for coffee pod machines. they are not made for use as "teabags with coffee" and they are not meant for keuring machines. if you put keurig cup inside a regualar drip coffee maker, would you expect coffee to come out the other end?

now for those who have a keurig machine and bought these, there is a solution. if you have one of the cartridges that allow you to use loose coffee, for example keurig my k-cup reusable coffee filter, then you can cut off one end of the pod and use the coffee. this will give the product as intended.

with that out of the way, let's turn to the product if you use it as intened or the "keurig workaround" i illustrated above.

each pod comes individually foil wrapped for freshness. when you open it, you are hit by the smell of strong coffee - perhaps even to the point of being pungent. when brewed, however, it is strong but not overpowering and actually has a surprising sweetness to it one would not have expected from the aroma. this is not a coffee that would appeal to those used to the mass produced variety or those who prefer a mild brew. it is fairly strong and best savored rather than guzzled. overall, a solid coffee experience.
name: Andy
